extracted.intended_audience: junior/senior mathematics undergraduates and instructors teaching introductory mathematical logic
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and foundational standards for constructing and using formal languages and developing an introductory undergraduate course/text in mathematical logic (sentential and first-order). Emphasizes syntax/semantics separation, formation rules, parsing, and pedagogical conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part description of a formal language
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal language should be described by (1) its set of symbols (alphabet); (2) the rules for forming grammatically correct finite sequences of symbols (well-formed formulas or wffs); and (3) the allowable translations between English and the formal language (the assignment of meaning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enderton states these three pieces explicitly and emphasizes that only in the third part is any meaning assigned to wffs. Examples and consequences are discussed: e.g., (A1 → (¬ A2)) is a wff under the formation rules; translations connect formal symbols to declarative English sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify the alphabet (logical vs nonlogical symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: The alphabet must list logical symbols (parentheses and sentential connectives ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔) and nonlogical symbols (sentence/propositional symbols A1, A2, ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical symbols have fixed roles in translations; sentence symbols are parameters whose translation is not fixed and may have many interpretations. The text distinguishes punctuation/logical symbols from nonlogical ones and treats their roles differently in semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation rules for well-formed formulas (wffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear recursive/grammatical rules that determine which finite sequences of symbols are well-formed formulas; examples show acceptable and unacceptable strings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate correct wffs (e.g., (A1 → (¬ A2))) and incorrect expressions (e.g., ')) → A3'). The book develops recursive/formal constructions and later proves unique readability; it also presents a parsing algorithm (Section 1.2) to recognize wffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique-readability / no-symbol-is-a-sequence-of-others requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Require that no one symbol be a finite sequence of other symbols so that finite sequences of symbols are uniquely decomposable (unique readability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enderton explains the assumption explicitly: e.g., demand that A3 ≠ (¬, A4, (( ). This guarantees that if (a1,...,am) = (b1,...,bn) with each ai and bj a symbol, then m = n and ai = bi. See Chapter 0 Lemma 0A and the unique readability theorems in later sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of syntax and semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish clearly between syntactic specification (symbols and formation rules) and semantics (the assignment of meaning / translations into English).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enderton emphasizes that one could manipulate wffs knowing only syntax (pieces 1 and 2) but meaning is only introduced in the third piece. This separation underlies later proofs (e.g., soundness/completeness) and motivates providing both formation and translation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and number of sentence symbols (design tradeoffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to include infinitely many distinct sentence symbols (A1, A2, ...) or to use a single symbol with notation like primes; document tradeoffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text discusses alternatives: using one symbol with primes reduces number of symbols but using distinct An is more convenient; allowing arbitrary (possibly uncountable) sets of sentence symbols affects later results (notably Section 1.7). Authors should state which choice they adopt and reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: decompose into atomic parts where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating natural-language sentences into the formal language, prefer breaking sentences down into atomic parts and using connectives (e.g., use (¬K) rather than inventing a new atomic symbol J for 'not K').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enderton gives the chemist examples explicitly (K for 'Traces of potassium were observed'; (¬K) for 'not observed') and contrasts creating new symbols vs decomposition. This is recommended to keep the logical structure explicit and manipulable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-functionality / determine compound truth from atomic parts
rubrics_metrics.description: For the sentential connectives, the truth or falsity of any compound formula must be computable immediately from the truth values of its atomic parts; truth tables / truth assignments should be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enderton constructs truth tables (Table I) showing how compound sentences' truth values follow from atomics. He stresses that this is a design feature: 'whenever we are given the truth or falsity of the atomic parts, we can then immediately calculate the truth or falsity of the compound.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide parsing algorithm and demonstration of unique decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Include an explicit parsing algorithm for the language so that wffs and their syntactic structure can be recognized and parsed; prove unique readability (parsing determinism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections referenced: Sentential parsing algorithm (Section 1.3) and parsing algorithm in first-order logic (Section 2.3). The book gives concrete parsing methods and proves unique readability (see Chapter 0 references and Section 1.4 on induction/recursion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses and notation conventions (or alternative Polish notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt conventions for parentheses to disambiguate formulas, or alternatively adopt Polish (prefix) notation as a choice; state the convention clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enderton shows conventional infix notation with parentheses and mentions Polish notation as an alternative; he also addresses use of parentheses in Table II and explains the role of punctuation in formation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical markings for exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: In the textbook, mark exercises with boldface numerals if their results are used in the exposition, and mark unusually challenging exercises with an asterisk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the Preface: 'If the exercise bears a boldface numeral, then the results of that exercise are used in the exposition in the text. Unusually challenging exercises are marked with an asterisk.' Instructors/readers should use these markings to prioritize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites and how to use preliminary material (Chapter 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: State expected background and indicate how to use preliminary set-theory material: the book is intended for readers with some mathematical background; Chapter 0 is concise and intended for reference rather than initial study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preface: 'The book is intended for the reader who has not studied logic previously, but who has some experience in mathematical reasoning. There are no specific prerequisites aside from a willingness to function at a certain level of abstraction and rigor. Chapter 0 gives a concise summary... It is suggested that the reader, instead of poring over this chapter at the outset, simply refer to it if and when issues ... arise.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible course organization (instructor options)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the organization flexible for instructors by indicating optional paths (via footnotes at many section starts) so courses of different lengths (quarter vs semester) can be adapted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preface explains three global changes including increased flexibility: 'Footnotes at the beginning of many of the sections indicate optional paths the instructor — or the independent reader — might choose to take.' The Preface also suggests typical coverage targets for a quarter or semester.
